newsitem.title: USA: Small guys defy odds, Internet providers double in '96.
newsitem.headline: Small guys defy odds, Internet providers double in '96.

text.p: The number of Internet service providers doubled to about 3,100 this year, according to Boardwatch Magazine, defying predictions the entry of larger companies and the move to $19.95 flat-rate pricing would slash the number of providers.

Small internet access firms are popping up across the United States to offer consumers more personal and sometimes cheaper Internet access as an alternative to the corporate powerhouses dominating the industry.
The number of Internet service providers, or ISPs, doubled to about 3,100 this year, according to the latest issue of Boardwatch, which provides a comprehensive listing of U.S. access providers.

Industry giants, like AT&T Corp.'s AT&T Worldnet and Netcom On-Line Communications Inc., command the lion's share of subscribers, with upwards of 500,000 subscribers each. And online services America Online Inc., Compuserve Corp. and Prodigy, have millions of customers.
The average ISP has only about 2,200 subscribers, a measure of how small most players remain. Instead of competing on price, they focus on other features like customer service and easy access.
"The smaller ISPs tend to do a better job of hand-holding people onto the Internet," said Jack Rickard, publisher of Boardwatch, based in Littleton, Colo.

"We hear stories of people driving out to (a subscriber's) house, setting them up and demo-ing in their living rooms," he said of demonstrations of how the service works. "You can't do that on a national scale."
Customer service is one of the biggest problems for the large firms, which often contract with other firms to provide customer assistance.

"Because of who they are, they are attracting the less sophisticated user, so they spend eight or 10 hours on the phone with a customer trying to get them online -- only to get $20 a month from them (in subscription fees)," Rickard said.
And that's often after expensive national advertising campaigns, massive free mailings of installation disks and CD-ROMs and free introductory online hours.

In contrast, explained Jill Loesberg, a research assistant at consultant Gerard, Klauer and Mattison in New York, the small provider grabs new subscribers by word of mouth or by placing a classified ad in a local newspaper.

Some are increasingly willing to price their service below the industry standard of $19.95 per month for unlimited use. A major New York radio station is carrying an advertisement for a service offering unlimited Internet access at $11.95 a month.

Further, logjams are increasing on bigger services as hundreds of thousands of users sign on at once during peak hours. Computer users are frustrated by busy signals, while others are disconnected during online sessions.
"Until the busy signals go away, there is going to be greater viability for these smaller companies," said Gregory Wester, Yankee Group's Research Director of Internet market strategy.
Rickard predicts growth in ISPs will continue for another year or two as the Internet lures more users.
But some analysts believe the growth may slow sooner as major players continue to grow, regional Bell phone companies enter the business and industry consolidation accelerates.
"There will be consolidation," Loesberg said. "People will migrate to AOL (America Online)" where people can get proprietary content in addition to a connection to the Internet.
America Online offers hundreds of special catagories of news, entertainment, weather, and investor information that are only available to AOL subscribers.
Perhaps the most daunting barrier for smaller ISPs is cash to finance further growth. "If you're a small shop, you can't fund your own development," Yankee Group's Wester said.

"If you're really lucky, you find a sugar daddy to buy you out. But in many cases these small ISPs simply don't have anything worth buying besides the net present value of the revenue stream of their customer (lists)."
